Home Instrument Evidence Framework Story Question GitHub
ONE ENGINE / TWO OPERATING MODES
Run one workflow. Or evaluate it as a grid.
A production workflow and an experiment use the same compiler, jobs, attempts, ledger, and policy controls. Fix the factors and the engine runs one cell. Vary them and it runs a controlled grid. Compare the cells, adapt one variable, and the grid becomes a campaign.
See the shared engine ↓ See the autonomy boundary →
OPERATE / FIXED ASSIGNMENT
1 cell
Execute the selected workflow.
Model, condition, policy, and constraints each have one active value.
EXPERIMENT / VARIED FACTORS
G cells
Execute controlled variants.
The factor cross-product creates cells; every cell enters the same workflow engine.
Who this is for: Organizations operating AI workflows at scale, from human-assisted engineering sessions to bounded autonomous pipelines. The current evidence is drawn from Python/Flask REST APIs and TypeScript/Node.js; validate the instrument in other domains before adopting its policy candidates.
Framework receipt
What is measured [M] Observed cost, outcome, narration, and cache fields from the corpus (1,067 story sessions, 7 models). What is computed [C] First-pass quality, Grit, cost per accepted outcome, WOC ratio — derived from the measured fields. What is modeled [P]/[X] β context inflation, EPM energy horizon, batch/cascade/SLA extensions — calibrated inputs and assumptions, not measured outcomes. Limitation A rule's premise being measured does not make the rule measured; rules not run as policy arms remain proposals. See The Evidence for verdicts.
WORKFLOW COMPILER / OPERATING MODES
One execution engine,
from cell to campaign.
A fixed assignment produces one workflow cell. Factor levels produce a grid of cells. Both compile into the same jobs and attempts; only the grid adds cross-arm comparison and adaptation.
OPERATE Fixed factor assignment → 1 cell
Run the workflow with one selected model, condition, policy, seed, and set of constraints.
EXPERIMENT Factor levels → G cells
Expand the same workflow across the product of active factor levels. Each assignment is one controlled cell.
same execution engine
01 / DECLARE Cell
Workflow, factor assignment, instrumentation, budget, and deadline.
02 / ORDER Compile
Validate dependencies and produce the executable DAG.
03 / CONTROL Jobs
Materialize work with a policy arm and operating limits.
04 / EXECUTE Attempts
Model calls, tools, retries, timing, tokens, and outcomes.
05 / RECORD Ledger
Append-only events shared by operations and experiments.
OBSERVE / MEASUREMENT
Measurement rules turn ledger fields into named information: first-pass quality, cost, grit, uncertainty, and value.
CONTROL / POLICY
Control rules consume available information to route, retry, escalate, budget, or halt work inside the running workflow.
LEARN / CAMPAIGN
When G > 1, compare policy arms, change one factor, and emit the next grid. The winning arm is already executable.
A production workflow is one cell. An experiment is a controlled grid of those same cells. A campaign uses their evidence to revise the next workflow policy.
G × N × M = instrumented evidence surface
G
Grid breadth: the product of active factor levels, such as model × condition × policy × seed.
N
Workflow depth: linked sessions or stages whose accumulated effects must remain visible.
M
Measurement breadth: independent angles applied to each stage, from correctness to cost and recovery.
G×N×M
Adding a factor level multiplies cells; adding a stage or measurement expands every cell.
1 / SELECT OR VARY Fixed factors produce one cell. Varied factors produce G cells without changing the workflow executor.
2 / EXECUTE AND RECORD Every cell becomes jobs and attempts that emit append-only events to the same ledger.
3 / MEASURE AND CONTROL Measurement rules produce information. Admissible control rules consume it inside the running workflow.
4 / COMPARE AND ADAPT Grids compare arms. Campaigns alter one factor and run the next evidence-acquisition pass.
FIELD MAP / EIGHT PLANES
Eight planes, one dependency direction.
The instrument is modular but not flat: the eight package planes form a dependency chain, and control consumes the information the lower planes produce. A plane's state is either instrumented (built and measured), proposed (designed but not run), or decided (a verdict binds it).
The eight planes (source: ARCHITECTURE.md)
Figure F1. The eight planes (core → experiment → measurement → runtime → adapters → knowledge → reporting → control → apps). One dependency direction, shown as a flow: core is the only foundation, and control is the only plane that consumes information. The diagram explains dependency direction; it makes no performance or capability claim.
[P] architecture source: ARCHITECTURE.md ref: svg-marker-flow.html, svg-filter-focus.html
The instrument cycle (Framework)
Figure F2. The instrument cycle — derive is the only path into policy, and a control rule whose requirements are not measured cannot be written. The red gate on the derive → write-policy arrow is that rejection.
[P] method ref: svg-marker-flow.html
TWO MODES / ONE ENGINE
One engine, two operating modes.
A fixed factor assignment produces one cell; a factor cross-product produces G cells. Both converge on the same compile → jobs → attempts → ledger path; only the grid branches to compare and adapt.
Fixed assignment → one cell; factor cross-product → G cells
Figure F3. One execution engine, two operating modes — both inputs converge on the same cell → compile → jobs → attempts → ledger path, and only the grid branches to compare and adapt. The written compiler/runtime, with no business KPI.
[P] compiler/runtime ref: svg-marker-flow.html
AUTONOMY / PROPOSED NOT RUN
A bounded-autonomy envelope.
The human policy boundary sits outside; inside it, declared constraints bound execution and independent verification. Exits are accept, reject/rework, or halt/escalate. Typed checkpoints remain proposed capability, not a run state.
Bounded-autonomy envelope
Figure F4. The bounded-autonomy envelope — a policy/architecture explanation. The typed-checkpoint cell is explicitly PROPOSED (amber, glowing), distinguished from the run-state cells.
[P] policy/architecture ref: svg-pattern-surface.html, svg-filter-focus.html
AUTHORITY / HUMAN CONTROL POINTS
Autonomy is bounded,
not human-free.
The agent may operate the workflow, but people define its objective, information requirements, policy, budget, and intervention conditions. Exceptions cross the boundary; routine work does not.
HUMAN CONTROL PLANE
Set objectives and specifications · approve policy arms · allocate budgets · define acceptance and escalation thresholds · review exceptions
authorize ↓ evidence and exceptions ↑
BOUNDED AUTONOMOUS WORKFLOW policy acts only inside declared limits
Admit
Route
Execute
Verify
Retry
Escalate
budget deadline quality SLA attempt limit required information
Accepted outcome → downstream system
Verified routine work continues without waiting for per-action human approval.
Exception → human adjudication
Policy uncertainty, exhausted budgets, failed verification, and material risk leave the autonomous boundary.
Assisted
The agent proposes work; a person approves consequential actions.
Supervised
The agent executes routine work; a person reviews outcomes and exceptions.
Bounded autonomous
The policy routes, retries, and escalates inside explicit limits; people govern the boundary.
Human involvement is itself a policy factor. A grid can compare approval points, intervention thresholds, escalation routes, and autonomy levels using the same workflow engine above.
ECONOMIC INPUTS / MEASURED AND MODELED
Separate what is measured,
controlled, and modeled.
Observed cost, outcome, and narration fields come from 227 historical experiment worktrees. Retry rate is a workload input until the attempt ledger measures it directly. Modeling parameters (β, EPM) are calibrated to your codebase and energy market. Separating observations, controls, and assumptions is the difference between deterministic budgeting and surprise overruns.
Augmented Workforce (Rules 1–5)
human + AI / per session
These drive the human+AI cost model. Teams using AI coding assistants interact with these every session.
C₀
Which model you call. $0.005 to $1.01 per session. Your primary cost lever. Two-way door – switch per task type.
Observed Two-way door
C₀ sub-lever
Cache Strategy. Cache write strategy: Store context at $3.75/Mtok (Anthropic). Cache read strategy: Retrieve existing context at $0.14/Mtok (DeepSeek default). Two-way door — measure your cache hit rate before committing. If <50% reuse, switch to cache-read.
Controlled Two-way door
P
Whether it produces working code. DeepSeek: 72% general pass rate with correct env. Pin frameworks to maximize this. Drives your retry overhead.
Observed Verification gate
ε
How much it narrates. Measured flail rates: 8.4% (DeepSeek) to 50% (GPT-5.5). Narration penalty: 0.3% to 30%. Pay only when you need auditable reasoning.
Measured Selection
β
Context inflation per line. Compounds quadratically through the Snowball Rule (N²). Default 0.001 — calibrate to your codebase growth rate.
Modeled One-way door
v
Code velocity per session. How much code you generate per session. Higher velocity accelerates the N² compounding.
Controlled One-way effect
EPM(t)
Energy price trajectory. Local energy markets determine long-term compute prices. IEA baseline: 1.6%/yr. Hedge scenario: 2.5%/yr.
Modeled One-way horizon
Autonomous Workloads (Rules 6–9)
bounded autonomy / per job
These drive the bounded autonomous cost model. Routine jobs run inside the declared policy; failed verification, exhausted limits, and material uncertainty return to the human control plane above.
C₀
Baseline cost per job. Same model cost lever as augmented, applied to a single autonomous unit of work. $0.001 to $1.01 per job depending on model tier.
Observed Two-way route
b
Batch fraction. What % of jobs run in batch mode. Batch gives 50% discount: D(b) = 1 − b×0.5. Trade-off: longer completion time.
Controlled Autonomous door
r
Retry rate. Fraction of jobs that fail first-pass and require another attempt or escalation. The calculator begins with an 11.5% scenario; replace it with your attempt-ledger rate before making a policy decision.
Scenario input Escalation gate
Eₔ
Escalation cost multiplier. How many × more expensive the escalation tier is vs the base model. Price ratio: 28.2× (DeepSeek → GPT-5.6), 68.7× (DS → Claude). Design for <1% escalation to human.
Modeled Autonomous door
W
Workload volume. Jobs per day processed autonomously. Throughput limit: T max = Budget / C job . Double the budget, double the capacity.
Controlled Budget ceiling
EPM(t)
Energy price trajectory. Same multiplier as augmented. Applies to both the base job cost and the retry/escallation overhead.
Modeled One-way horizon

POLICY / RULE STATUS
Ten rules, three statuses.
Each rule is grouped by its current status: instrumented (its inputs and premise are measured), proposed (modeled or designed but not run as an arm), or decided (a verdict binds it). A rule's premise being measured does not make the rule measured — a policy becomes decided only when it is run as an arm and compared.
[M] instrumented
1. Grit (Ground-Truth Integrity)
Default to models that keep correctness under degraded input.
Source and limits
Inputs: test-executed success under 10 perturbation operators ([M]). Evidence class [M]/[C]. Limitation: single-session + story corpus; not a universal trait. Next test: strength-grid live run.

POLICY / PROPOSED CONTROL RULES
Turn observed patterns into
policy arms to test.
These are organized across three provenance tiers. Observed patterns are directly visible in the measurement corpus (227 historical single-session perturbation experiments + 1,067 multi-session story sessions). Derived metrics compute operational quantities from those observations. Modeled extensions project beyond what the experiment directly measures.
Selection and verification
Choose for resilience, explanation overhead, and working outcomes.
1
Grit (Ground-Truth Integrity). Default to models that maintain correctness when given degraded, contradictory, or incomplete instructions. If a model flails under perturbation — producing zero code despite high token output — it has low Grit. Don't use it for unsupervised work. The 10 perturbation operators measure Grit across three perturbation classes: specification corruption, objective mutation, and process perturbation. Concept: Grit (Ground-Truth Integrity) · Lever: C₀
2
The Explanation Tax. Rule 1 selects models that CAN code under degraded input. Rule 2 measures what their resilience COSTS — the flail rate (sessions producing zero code) and narration penalty (overhead on successful sessions). Measured: Claude 11% flail, 8% penalty. DeepSeek 8% flail, 0.0% penalty. For auditable work, the tax is insurance. For routine tasks, it's waste. Concept: Explanation Tax · Lever: ε
5
The First-Pass Rule. Price the accepted outcome, not the prompt. A cheaper model can lose its price advantage through failed verification, retries, and escalation. Derive first-pass quality from attempt number, acceptance, and an independent evaluator; then track it by task type, model, policy, and time window. Do not substitute a narrated report failure rate for an attempt-ledger measurement. Concept: Cost-Per-Accepted-Outcome / First-Pass · Lever: P, retry rate
Compounding economics
Model codebase, energy, and outcome effects before they become architecture.
3
The Snowball Rule. Your codebase grows with every session. Each new line of generated code increases the context window for every future session. This isn't additive – it's quadratic. The more you build, the more each subsequent build costs. Measured: story cost roughly doubles across the five-session arc ($0.16 → $0.34, a 2.13× Snowball). The β term compounds per-session — model the curve before you commit to an architecture. This is a one-way door. Concept: Snowball Effect (N²) · Lever: β, v · Formula: C(N,v) = C₀ × EPM(N) × [N + β·v·N(N−1)/2]
4
The EPM Horizon Rule. Energy costs are the inflation rate of AI compute. Local energy markets – not global averages – determine your long-term prices. A team in Texas (ERCOT grid) faces different EPM growth than one in Frankfurt (ENTSO-E) or Singapore. Find the year your geographic energy costs flip your model selection. Hedge before that point. EPM(t) = 1.00 + r(t−2024) where r depends on your region. Concept: EPM Horizon · Lever: EPM(t)
10
The Outcome Multiplier. The goal isn't to minimize cost – it's to maximize outcomes per dollar. Business Value Index = Total Successful Outcomes / Total AI + Human Cost. A 2× BVI means twice the work for the same cost. A 10× BVI unlocks new business models. Extension Concept: Business Value · Lever: BVI
Autonomous operations
Bound batch, budget, escalation, and SLA behavior.
6
The Batch Discount. Batch processing is 50% cheaper but has a 72-hour horizon. If your task doesn't need a response in <4 hours, run in batch. Monitor queue depth. Extension Modeled Concept: Batch Economics · Lever: b, Q
7
The Budget Ceiling. Your maximum throughput is set by your budget, not your infrastructure. Max jobs/day = Budget / (Cost per job × (1 + retry_rate)). Double your budget, double your capacity – zero hiring required. Extension Modeled Concept: Throughput Cap · Lever: W (jobs/day)
8
The Cascade Rule. In autonomous workloads, failures auto-escalate through model tiers: Flash → Sonnet → Opus → Human. A 1% escalation to human review can double your total cost. Design for <1% escalation. Extension Modeled Concept: Auto-Escalation · Lever: Eₔ (28.2× price ratio: DS → GPT-5.6)
9
The SLA Buffer. Actual batch completion time = (Queue_length × Avg_job_time) + (Retry_buffer × retry_rate). Never batch jobs with an SLA less than 2× your observed queue depth. Always have an on-demand fallback. Extension Modeled Concept: Batch SLA · Lever: Slack Buffer
Observed from the experiment corpus (cost variation, outcome retention, recovery overhead). Derived metrics (Grit, WOC, cost per outcome). Modeling extensions (Snowball, EPM, batch, cascade, SLA, BVI) are modeled projections — not independently tested.

Cache Strategy
Three-layer caching turns the provider economics in your favor. Each layer compounds on the one below.
Layer 1
Gateway Exact-Match. Return cached responses for identical prompts within TTL. Zero token cost. 80–95% savings on repeated prompts.
Layer 2
Provider Prefix Cache. Structure prompts so repeated prefixes hit the provider-side disk cache (DeepSeek, Anthropic). 50–90% savings on input tokens.
Layer 3
Semantic Cache. Match semantically similar prompts with a threshold (embedding cosine similarity ≥ 0.97). 20–60% savings on similar-but-not-identical prompts.
Critical rule: Static content before dynamic content — one dynamic field in the wrong position invalidates the prefix cache. Place system prompts, tool definitions, and static instructions first. Append user input last.
Two-Way Door
Cache Write vs Read. Cache writes preserve context but cost $3.75/Mtok (Anthropic). Cache reads retrieve context at $0.14/Mtok (DeepSeek). Measure your cache hit rate. If under 50%, switch to cache-read mode. If over 80%, cache-write pays for itself. Toggle per workstream.
Simulated Model Routing
Routing here isn't a vendor diagram — it's computed. compute_routing() (in src/instrument/routing.py ) reads the experiment corpus, groups sessions by task, and recommends per task a default model (cheapest that clears the correctness threshold) or an escalation model (when a higher-correctness model leads by a meaningful margin). It then simulates single-model vs grit-routed strategies across the whole corpus.
Routing chain: request → task classifier → computed default model → verification gate → escalate-on-margin
60–80% of requests are simple (classification, formatting, lookup). These should never touch a frontier model.
Tier 1 · Simple
~60% of volume. DeepSeek V3 / GPT-4o-mini / Claude Haiku. Classification, extraction, formatting, lookup.
Tier 2 · Moderate
~25% of volume. DeepSeek R1 / GPT-4o / Claude Sonnet. Code generation, structured reasoning, analysis.
Tier 3 · Complex
~15% of volume. GPT-5.6 / Claude Opus. Multi-step architecture, novel problem solving.
Budget Enforcement
Hard caps prevent runaway costs. These tools enforce limits at the gateway layer.
tokencap
Token-based rate limiting per key, per model, per time window. tokencap --key sk-xxx --limit 1M --window 1h --model gpt-5.6
token-limiter
Enforce max tokens per request. Reject before the provider sees it. token-limiter --model gpt-5.6 --max-input 128000 --max-output 16384
agentbudget
Per-agent cost ceilings with automatic escalation to human review. agentbudget --agent coding-agent --daily-cap $5.00 --on-exceed escalate

Subscription route: the same model runs through the Claude CLI adapter ( --backend claude_cli ) — subscription-safe, no per-token API spend.
Escalation Economics
When a cheap model fails, you pay the retry penalty — and you lose the verification the expensive model would have written. Here's what that actually costs.
Key metrics from 215 stories
Escalation multiplier (Eₔ) 50× (Luna → Sonnet 5)
Test coverage gap 17× (7 vs 122 tests/cell)
Sonnet vs DeepSeek gap 30× ($4.78 vs $0.16 per session)
Cost per escalation tier
Tier 1 (Luna) ~$0.09
Tier 2 (DeepSeek) ~$0.16
Tier 3 (Sonnet 5) ~$4.78
Verification depth 7 → 122 tests/story
The takeaway: The cascade doesn't just save money — it buys verification where it matters. Route the happy path to Luna, the refactor-heavy work to DeepSeek, and reserve Sonnet for the safety-critical edge cases that would cost more to miss than to test.

Narration flail rates 6–50% across models.
